articles.text: U.S. Surgeon General’s report What follows below is based on the recently published U.S. Surgeon General Advisory (a public statement that calls the American people’s attention to an urgent public health issue and provides recommendations), and is directed most particularly at parents of children or adolescents. It summarizes, paraphrases, or quotes the most relevant and applicable information from the Advisory, which is available online in full, or as a summary of its main points. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy, after an examination of the still ongoing research regarding the impact of social media on children and adolescents, concluded that platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube should come with a warning label stating they are associated with significant mental health harm for children and adolescents. In a sense, the Advisory is a cautionary tale, part of a suggested national dialogue, which informs us that 95% of teenagers, ages 13-17, use social media daily (the average is 3.5 hours), with more than a third saying they use social media “almost constantly.” One in three adolescents report using such sites until midnight or beyond. One-in-four teens spend 5+ hours per day online, and one in seven spend 7+ hours. Onethird or more girls, ages 11-15, say they feel “addicted” to certain social media platforms, and over half of all teenagers indicate it would be “hard to give up.” The Advisory goes on to affirm that research has revealed that there are ample indicators that social media can have a profound risk of harm to the mental health and well-being of children and adolescents during critical stages of their lives. Youth, ages 10-19, are undergoing a highly sensitive period of brain development. This is a stage in life when change, both physically and mentally, is the constant. High risk-taking behaviors reach their peak, and well-being experiences reach their greatest fluctuations. Mental health challenges emerge, such as identity, sense of self-worth, susceptibility to peer pressures, as well as peer opinions and comparisons, impulse control, plus the challenges of moderating social behavior. Teens also experience an increasing sensitivity to social rewards and punishment, thus intensifying their responses to social media. Research has also found that among youth there is a relationship between excessive social media use and poor sleep quality, reduced sleep duration, sleep difficulties and depression. And there is the chilling fact that harmful content continues to be easily accessible by children and adolescents on social media. While platforms can be hubs used for the sharing of ideas, nurturing and sustaining communication with friends and family, they also can possess a dark curtain of anonymity. Social media sites can embody a cartography of predatory behavior and interactions perpetrated by malicious actors whose intent is to target vulnerable young people. Hiding in the darkest corners online are individuals/ adults seeking to exploit or extort risk-taking children and adolescents sexually (using intimate images) or financially. Nearly six out of ten adolescent girls say they have been contacted by strangers in ways that make them feel uncomfortable. Some social media platforms, targeting adolescent girls, show depictions of self-harm acts such as partial asphyxiation, cutting leading to excessive bleeding, suicide pacts, images of disordered eating habits, and ever present is potential tragedy. Some 64% of adolescents are “often” or “sometimes” exposed to hate-based content, and one third of girls of color report exposure to racist language or content. Cyber-bullying has been linked to depression among children and adolescents causing negative social comparisons, especially among girls and sexual minorities (LGBTQ+). This year, the parade Grand Marshal will be Gray Cathrall, founder 26 years ago of the Piedmont Post, the community’s weekly print newspaper. As is tradition, Cathrall will be featured as a prominent rider near the front of the parade in one of the parade’s dignitary cars. The Piedmont Community Band, the city’s only musical organization that can claim a single rehearsal during the year, will celebrate its 40th anniversary as part of the city’s 4th of July parade this year. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – who can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led each year by Ken Kawaichi, who has the distinction of being the only person to march the length of the parade route backwards. Parade Committee Chair Kathy Kelleher wanted to give a special thanks to the committee members who volunteered to put on the parade this year. “It takes the entire committee’s hard work and dedication to get the parade to where it is. And we have an amazing committee that I need to thank for that,” she said. In 2020, the parade was canceled because of COVID-19 concerns, and returned in 2022 with a mix of eagerness and cautious hesitancy. This will be the parade’s third year back since it was canceled, and the event is poised to be the parade’s first full-fledged return, according to organizers. articles.text: Keeping with tradition, the City of Piedmont has hired a herd of nearly 200 goats to control the weeds in Moraga Canyon ahead of the upcoming fire season. At 6:15 a.m. last Wednesday, June 26, the goats rushed out of their trailer in a flurry of black, white and brown fur as they filed onto the hillside behind the Corporation Yard. The four-legged grazers will be working in this area for approximately two weeks, according to the Piedmont Public Works Department. After their task is complete, the pack of furry lawncare advocates will be moved across Moraga Avenue to Blair Park where they will continue their work. “It is kind of a common practice for managing open spaces, but it’s for good reason. It’s a great practice,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works for the City of Piedmont. Each year, the City of Piedmont competitively bids on the services of these goats in the employ of Ecosystem Concepts, a local vegetation management company. “The goats are very much in high demand for the same reasons we like them,” said Gonzales. “They’re very inexpensive. Ecologically, they’re One of the goats takes a break after a long day at work. Photos by Jesse Rosenberg A brown goat from Ecosystem Concepts, a local vegetation management company, scales a hill above Coaches Field with his herd. much better for the environment. They also do a lot of the things that you would otherwise have to do with mechanical equipment in areas that are very challenging to get into.” Ecosystem Concepts has set up a trailer where the goat herder will stay for the duration of the work. Additionally, a herding dog will also be present on-site to corral the goats when necessary. The herd’s vegetation-eating efforts are crucial to fire prevention, especially in the hot summer months. In the coming weeks, goats will chew their way through the overgrown brush, weeds and the lower limbs of trees behind the Corporation Yard to create a “fuel break” through which wildfires are less likely to burn. Officials hope that this effort will provide a critical buffer for homes up the hill in the event of a fire. “Our goal is to prevent fire from being able to spread from point A to point B around the City,” explained Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. The Fire Department has been working with the Public Works since April to prepare this area for several different vegetation management projects that will mitigate fire risk, including the arrival of the goats. “In this case, we don’t want the uphill travel of fire from a lower area in this topography up to the higher levels where there are residents and houses.” Gonzales estimates that the annual grazing will take between two to three weeks. Residents who want to see the herd are being advised to not park on dry grasses, block traffic or touch the goats. For more information about the goats and where to see them, please contact the Public Works Department at 420-3050. Goats team up to take down a bush.

articles.text: Lawyer representing neighbors receives no response from the city A group of homeowners is questioning the legality of a construction project on their street approved by the City of Piedmont’s Planning and Building Department. The project, located at 67-77 Wistaria Way, seeks to divide the vacant lot into two parcels, and its property owners will construct a new home on each parcel alongside a single auxiliary dwelling unit (ADU) on the property. Citizens residing adjacent to the property are being represented by Piedmont resident and lawyer Kurt Peterson of the law firm Peterson Martin Reynolds LLP. Peterson said he took the case because of the new legal challenge posed by the law related to the project — the California Housing Opportunity and More Efficiency (HOME) Act, also known as “SB9” after its designation before signing, “Senate Bill 9.” “I do a fair amount of real A photo of the wetlands located at Wistaria Way which flow into Wildwood Creek. Neighbors are concerned this new housing project could disrupt local flora. estate property work, and this sounded like an interesting legal project,” said Peterson. “SB 9 is a fairly new law. It hasn’t really Water flows down Wildwood Creek during the wet season and under a long-standing permanent bridge on the Wistaria Way property. been tested [...] And so whenever you see a new statutory scheme coming about, lawyers like to try to understand if it really meets the policy objectives that the law was intended to meet. And I don’t think this one does.” SB 9 was passed and signed by Governor Newsom in 2021. This bill went into effect on January 1, 2022. According to the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley, the law aims to address California’s housing crisis by allowing homeowners to divide their lot and construct up to four houses on a single-family parcel. When the legislation was passed, some heralded it as a significant win for zoning reform, paving the way for smallscale homebuilding in previously exclusionary areas. Others worried that the law would encourage speculation and unbridled expansion at the price of the character of the neighborhood and vulnerable residents. In a letter to the city dated August 23, 2023, Peterson outlined a four-pronged argument for why the city should reject the project’s application for a lot split, claiming that the project fails to meet the law’s site eligibility requirements, lot split requirements, non-compliance with objective standards as well as health and safety concerns of neighbors covered by California’s protective easement statutes.

articles.text: The popular First Fridays return to Chabot Space & Science Center just in time for summer. Beginning Friday, July 5, from 6 to 10 p.m. Chabot will be transformed on the first Friday of every month into a fun, interactive, science-filled playground for learners and weekend revelers of all ages to come together and discover, dance and dream. First Fridays have become a habit for families with K-12 children and toddlers, a popular date night for singles and couples, and a hangout for friends and colleagues. Visitors can surf through the stars in Chabot’s newly renovated Planetarium, strap in for some seriously exciting hands-on science, and be a part of the most stellar block party in the Galaxy. In addition to a wealth of regular exhibits and things to see and do, First Fridays includes DJs, food and beverages, and is open from 6-10 p.m. Admission is $10 adults, $5 kids/seniors and free for Chabot members. For more information and advance tickets, visit www.ChabotSpace.org. Visitors will explore the mysteries of the universe through interactive exhibits including the all-new NASA Ames Visitor Center, hands on activities and mesmerizing glowin-the-dark displays revealing the illuminating science behind why things glow. Guests can make and keep DIY glow-in-the-dark jewelry. Adults can enjoy a relaxing experience at Cosmos & Cocktails in the Courtyard.

articles.text: A recent Piedmont Middle School graduate, Gracey Ann Hatchell, will return to her old campus this summer to paint a mural with a marine conservation theme. Hatchell described her project to members of the Piedmont School Board on June 26, to get board approval for her project. The mural will meet the requirement for her to earn a Girl Scout Silver Award. Speaking remotely to the school board from Camp Augusta near Nevada City, Hatchell said, “This has been three years in the making, so it feels really good to present it to the board.” The goal of this project is to educate middle schoolers about making sustainable choices regarding the ocean and to promote overall ocean conservation. The mural will bring attention to the website seafoodwatch.com. Some of the criteria for earning a Girls Scout Silver Award are that a project must involve 50 hours of community service and make a lasting difference in the community. “One of the things that came up at the middle school site council was how to beautify the campus, and I think having a mural would fit that bill perfectly,” said A sketch of Hatchell’s mural design containing a shark, an octopus and a dolphin. “Greeting from the woodchips!” Hatchell addressed the school board, while connected to Camp Augusta’s WIFI. board member Cory Smegal. The mural will be located on the first floor of the school. The project is expected to take two weekends to clean and map out the mural, then to paint it onto the wall in layers. Hatchell received coaching from PMS Green Team teacher, John White, and more general support from science teacher, Laura Archer. She received approval from PMS administrators before taking the idea to the school board. “When I was a tiny four-yearold, with a pink bow on my head, I would drag my parents to the Monterey Bay Aquarium to see the Giant Pacific octopus and other creatures that were there,” said Hatchell. “My love of the ocean has very much defined me as a person,” she added.

articles.text: “Look out the window; everything’s different here,” my dad excitedly told me on the drive to my aunt’s house. This line was a favorite of my dad, an avid traveler. Anywhere we went, he encouraged me to look for the differences, and in doing so see what remains the same, what connects us. (Dad, I take credit for that last line but only because you never said it out loud. I’m just informing our audience.) Malaysia is a unique country by many measures, and it’s always incredible to visit, even if I’d rather stuff my face with kueh than pay attention to my surroundings. This time however, I kept my eyes open extra wide, just in case a global pandemic hit again and my next visit wouldn’t be for five years. One thing I noticed more than ever was the nature and atmosphere. Being a Californian, I thought I’d seen some pretty complex ecosystems. Imagine my shock when I saw monkeys playing near my grandfather’s memorial, or when I saw exotic fruits whose names were a mystery casually displayed at a local market, as well as fruits we rarely get treated to in the U.S. Everywhere I turn it is green. The natural beauty is so vibrant, enhanced by nearly 100 inches of rain each year, allowing an abundance of plants and animals to thrive. Coupled with the consistent 80°F heat year round, a trait almost exclusive to the equator, the variety of wildlife in Malaysia is unlike anywhere else in the world. The lush rainforests are home to an unparalleled array of biodiversity and complex ecosystems. From the proboscis monkey – the world’s largest – an almost extinct species that resides mostly in Malaysia, to the Hibiscus, its national flower, Malaysia is brimming with species unlike anything in California. Orchids, one of the most complex flowers in the world, have unique species in Malaysia, in sharp contrast to its four-foot Raffia Arnoli, nicknamed the ‘corpse flower’ due to the fact that besides being the largest flower in the world, it stinks of rotting flesh. Back in Kuala Lumpur, daily wet market vendors unload their goods. From fresh magosteen and custard apples to crisp greens, the wet market is a reflection of the connection to nature. And, who would I be if I didn’t mention the durian, king of fruits? Notoriously smelly and a dividing point between many Malaysians, durian is an integral part of our culture, from the No Durian signs on trains to durian dodol, a gluttonous candy made with the fleshy fruit. Late at night, the large, prickly fruits are bought, then brought home and broken apart with a knife. The fruits crack naturally, and the family swarms to get their hands on the fleshy, fragrant pods that encase large seeds, the aroma holding still in the air for time long after the last stone has been licked clean. Gathering around durian should be a family tradition. There is always an abundance of fresh vegetables at wet markets. In embracing the differences, I not only witnessed the striking contrasts between Malaysia and my home in California but also discovered the underlying threads that connect us all. Adopting my father’s frame of mind as I explored Malaysia not only broadened my horizons but also deepened my appreciation for the diversity of our world. As I carry these memories with me, I am reminded that in embracing the differences, we uncover the profound similarities that unite us all. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen fascinated by the gecko outside of her window. She is a regular contributor with the Piedmont Post. Monkeys play in the grass. Skyscrapers and foliage blend in harmony in Kuala Lumpur, the Capital of Malaysia.

articles.text: Emily Thompson School is out, the days are longer, and (hopefully) we are all enjoying some much-deserved rest. Summer is a time to decompress from the school year but it can also be a great time for academic enrichment. Finding balance is important, and by building some structure into the summer, students can rest and recuperate while also exploring interests, shoring up academic foundations, and preparing for the future. Our top recommendation is to use the summertime to read! Reading has numerous benefits, including increased comprehension, reduced stress levels, more vivid imagination, and higher levels of concentration. Students who already enjoy reading might use the summer to explore new or more challenging material. If reading isn’t your student’s favorite activity, set a small but consistent goal, such as 15 minutes or one chapter per day. Making reading a family activity can also be helpful. articles.text: Layth Haddawy with his silver medal at the USPA National Championship in Las Vegas. Piedmont High junior Layth Haddawy continues his ascent as a talented power lifter, recently competing in the United States Powerlifting Association National Championships in Las Vegas on June 24-28. In the Age 16-17 category at 132 pounds, Haddaway finished second of 10 athletes by hitting 309 pounds in the squat, 204 pounds on the bench press, a 419 pound dead lift, and the combined total of 932 pounds. Haddawy last competed in the USPA 2024 Spring Break back in April, increasing his squat 29 pounds, his dead lift nearly 50 pounds, and his combined weight up 73 pounds. “Since then, I’ve been sticking to a similar program. But this time, I was able to shoot my attempts at a higher weight. I was definitely happy to shoot what I wanted to and it was a good learning experience. I wish I could have lifted a higher total. The person who beat me was 11 and a half months older than me,” Haddawy added. The only category Haddawy was unable to improve with his bench press. He thinks the toll of pushing his 132-pound weight limit had something to do with it. Some of the common rigors for athletes like weight-lifters, wrestlers, and those in fighting sports are facing a difficult weight-cut down to a specific target. Leading up to his second official event ever, Haddawy had to drop pounds before weigh-ins. “I think I could’ve increased my total if I didn’t have a super harsh water-cut. On the final day, I had to sweat out two pounds of water the day before,” Haddawy said. He’s now focused on bumping up a weight class to the 148- pound category, giving him an opportunity to build more muscle after dealing with the constraint of competing at 132. “I’m going up a weight category. I haven’t really been able to put on much size over the last couple of months because of having to cut down to 132,” Haddawy said. With the National Championships being the second competitive event of his power lifting career, Haddawy knows he is learning a lot as he continues. “I think one thing that held me back was on my bench was figuring out a consistent technique. I feel my numbers didn’t go up because I got a bit stuck on trying to figure out my technique to a consistent level,” Haddawy. Layth found power lifting after competing on Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team last year. Instead of standing out on the field, he found he was always lifting more weight than his football teammates – leading him to Get Bent Gym in Oakland. “I’ve been lifting for a while, but I began taking powerlifting very seriously in November when the football season ended,” Haddawy said in April. “Throughout my life, I played all the team sports you can think of, but I never was great at any of them. But I realized, especially at football, I wasn’t ever the best guy on the field but I was always the strongest player on the team. I thought, if I’m too undersized for football, I should find something that fits me.” He looks ahead to the Iron Built Games on September 14 in Concord.

articles.text: Perhaps the lasting memory for the U.S. in the 2024 Copa América was manager Gregg Berhalter signaling to his team that Panama and Bolivia, teams in the same group as the U.S., were tied 1-1. Seconds later Uruguay scored to beat the U.S. The CONMEBOL Copa América group stage played out exactly how United States Men’s National Team fans were dreading. After opening the tournament with an expected 2-0 win over Bolivia, the Americans fell apart in a 2-1 loss to Panama, and then closed with an ugly 1-0 loss to No. 15 Uruguay on Monday, July 1. They finished third in the group and out of competition. The United States became the first host nation in Copa América’s 108-year history to get knocked out in the Group Stage. Photo courtesy of Sporting News Is it time to turn the page on United States manager Gregg Berhalter? Against Panama, the U.S. entered as the undoubted favorite but a red card on Tim Weah in the 18th minute was the start of the letdown. Although Folarin Balogun scored to put the U.S. ahead in the 22nd minute, they conceded to Cesar Blackman just four minutes later. Panama finished the night with a dominant 74 percent of possession, notching 13 shot attempts to the States’ six. While one man down, the Stars and Stripes never figured out a way to deal with the disadvantage. It led to a do-or-die game on Monday with Uruguay. With everything on the line, the United States continued its lackluster ways with just three shots going on target for a second-consecutive game. Mathias Olivera’s game-winning goal in the 66th was a questionable non-offside call, but it wouldn’t have mattered. With Panama beating Bolivia 3-1, the United States would have needed three goals to achieve second place in Group C. Perhaps the most embarrassing moment was manager Gregg Berhalter signaling to his team that Bolivia and Panama were tied 1-1—meaning the U.S. briefly held second-place. But just seconds after the camera cut away from Berhalter, Olivera put in the winner. The United States’ inability to win big games and get out of Group C was a strong indictment on Berhalter and the roster dubbed, “the Golden Generation.” The question remains: Is the problem the U.S. coaching leadership, or is it a lineup that has failed to take the next step with its development. Aside from being successful in their confederation’s tournaments, like the CONCACAF Nations League and Gold Cup, the United States has routinely struggled to pull off wins against teams outside its confederation. It was a tournament marred with controversy after Gio Reyna was benched, leading to a rift in the locker room. Despite the situation with Reyna, the United States Soccer Federation elected to extend Berhalter’s contract as head coach. A little league is a league for youth baseball and softball players. PBSF also brings more youth into their baseball and softball games, umpires. Umpires are like referees for baseball and softball. Now, PBSF has made it so kids as young as 10 can umpire the age division below them. After the training I soon got to umpire my first baseball game (I only umpire baseball) . It was very fun making the calls, like if a runner made it to first base in time or not in time. At the time of publishing I have umpired 4 games. Umpiring has its upside and downside. An upside is that you make money. $30 is not that much for adults but, for kids that is a lot. Plus, it is a great way to make friends. The other umpires that you work with normally are pretty similar to you. It’s a great way to join the baseball community. Also, your decisions stand and the players have to follow it. So you do not have to argue, which saves you a lot of effort. The downside is that umpiring is pretty exhausting. You have to stand for 90 minutes and you have to pay attention for 90 minutes. Also, sometimes the coaches and players get mad at you. One reason they get mad at you is when they think you called something wrong. Another reason they get mad is when a rule is broken and the coach and players don’t know that rule. They get mad because they think what just happened is normal and you called it out or safe differently then normal. Overall, I think umpiring is an awesome experience. It is so fun. I would recommend umpiring if you are a sporty kid who wants to make some money. Jonah Kerr is a 5th grader at Havens Elementary School.

Seconds later Uruguay scored to beat the U.S. By Jonathan Comeaux The CONMEBOL Copa América group stage played out exactly how United States Men’s National Team fans were dreading. After opening the tournament with an expected 2-0 win over Bolivia, the Americans fell apart in a 2-1 loss to Panama, and then closed with an ugly 1-0 loss to No. 15 Uruguay on Monday, July 1. They finished third in the group and out of competition. The United States became the first host nation in Copa América’s 108-year history to get knocked out in the Group Stage. Against Panama, the U.S. entered as the undoubted favorite but a red card on Tim Weah in the 18th minute was the start of the letdown. Although Folarin Balogun scored to put the U.S. ahead in the 22nd minute, they conceded to Cesar Blackman just four minutes later. Panama finished the night with a dominant 74 percent of possession, notching 13 shot attempts to the States’ six. While one man down, the Stars and Stripes never figured out a way to deal with the disadvantage. It led to a do-or-die game on Monday with Uruguay. articles.text: Our second of five features of trails around Lake Tahoe continues with the Five Lakes Trail in Olympic Valley near Alpine Meadows on the northern side of Lake Tahoe. Some back country hikers will try to get to this location quickly in the morning to camp out next to three swimmable lakes. You’ll require just over an hour worth of hiking to reach one of the most picturesque dayhikes in California. The Five Lakes Trail is a 4.8 mile hike in total and provides around 1,100 feet of elevation gain in Tahoe National Forest’s Granite Chief Wilderness. It’s a good location to get accustomed with hiking in high elevation. Our day starts at 6,450 feet of altitude, topping out at near 7,600 feet. It also connects with the historic Pacific Crest Trail. The trail goes on the southern ends of the KT-22 and Washeshu mountain peaks. To your left will be views of the pine-treed strewed mountains of Scott Peak and the mosaic of jagged rock cliff faces toward Ward Peak. This location is surrounded by resorts and the tourist towns of Truckee, Tahoe City, Kings Beach and other North Lake Tahoe destinations, so the hike can be a traffic jam. We passed 105 other hikers in the trek toward the summit and another 51 on the way back to the car. You’ll to have patience while passing others. . Long portions of the trail are less than six-feet wide, requiring you to step aside for groups. I passed at least three groups of 10 or more people and many families. Faster hikers may find themselves behind slower traffic without a clear pathway around. But at the summit, a group of five alpine lakes awaiting. Despite the foot traffic, you can easily find your own area on one of the three swimmable lakes. This lake is more marshy but equally as picturesque. articles.text: By Allyson Aleksey Aurora Theatre Company’s production of Lifespan of a Fact, written by Jeremy Kareken, David Murrel and Gordon Ferrell, will be performed through July 21. The critically acclaimed 2018 Broadway play follows the demanding and high-stakes world of publishing. Magazine editor Emily Penrose hires a young, determined fact-checker named Jim Fingal to work on a groundbreaking essay written by the famous author John D’Agata. Based on the true story of D’Agata’s essay What Happens There, the show blurs the lines between fact and fiction as young reporter Jim finds that the the legendary essayist bends the truth in his own writing. The cast includes Hernán Angulo as Jim and Carrie Paff as Emily. The production is directed by Jessica Holt in her Aurora Theatre directing debut Post-show discussions of Aurora’s production of Lifespan of a Fact will be led by Aurora staff and members of the creative team, joined by the actors on July 2, 10 and 18. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024-season/the-lifespan-of-a-fact. articles.text: Bear Valley Music Festival begins July 21, marking the 55th anniversary of the iconic outdoor music festival along Highway 4. All concerts are tucked inside a large tent that holds 500 guests in the outdoor wonderland of Bear Valley, California. The festival features an eclectic variety of music from 80’s tribute bands to classic Jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy. We’ve been doing it for 55 years and are excited to celebrate that milestone this summer. From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone,” said Board of Directors president Julia Mee. Music Director Alexander Mickelthwate returns for his second year. The British band English Beat will open the festival with an energetic mix of musical styles, fronted by showman Dave Wakeling. English Beat fuses Latin, ska, pop, soul, reggae and punk rock and released three studio albums in the early 1980s, including I Just Can’t Stop It (1980), Wha’ppen? (1981) and Special Beat Service (1982), as well as a string of singles, including “Mirror in the Bathroom”, “Save It for Later”, “I Confess”, “Too Nice to Talk To”, “Can’t Get Used to Losing You“ and “Hands Off...She’s Mine.” Opening weekend will also include Steel ’n’ Chicago, a tribute to both Steely Dan and Chicago, and Deja Vu, a tribute to Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young. The Laurence Hobgood Trio, a Jazz ensemble, performs on Wednesday, July 26. The festival runs through Sunday, August 6. For the full festival lineup and tickets. visit www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org.

articles.text: Organist Jonathan Dimmock performs every Saturday at the Legion of Honor. Visit the Legion of Honor in San Francisco on Saturday afternoons and enjoy a free organ concert by Jonathan Dimmock or Angela Kraft Cross. Residents of all nine Bay Area counties, including Alameda, receive free admission to Legion of Honor in San Francisco on Saturdays. Visit the museum during operating hours and view its permanent collection galleries. Visitors ages 17 and under always receive free admission to the permanent collection galleries. Included with free admission is an organ concert every Saturday at 4 p.m. Dimmock is a graduate of Oberlin and Yale, and the first American to hold the prestigious position of organ scholar of Westminster Abbey. articles.text: Review by Paul Hertelendy In writing a symphony, composers are like architects designing a new city. But not Gustav Mahler. In his Symphony No. 3 he created a musical metropolis of 100 minutes, running the length of two or three others’ symphonies. The oversize orchestra, with doubled winds and harps, a paired set of timpani within a seven-member augmented percussion group, plus singers, add up to a bulging score more like four symphonies in one. The extravagance was unprecedented, with no regard for production costs. At the end, like the cherry on the sundae, three percussionists haul out oversize cymbals two feet in diameter for a single, colossal crash. Created mostly in summer “holidays” of 1895-96, the work had Mahler in an unparalleled burst of inspiration, wherein parts of the resultant score actually had to be siphoned off to enter his next (fourth) symphony. Holed up in a small summer cabin by the Salzburg-region’s lakes, Mahler required absolute silence, with helpers chasing away birds and noisy children. Mahler’s musical metropolis was above all pastoral, with subtitles alluding to summer, flowers, animals, love, even angels. And yet the five-movement opus is bursting with passion and drama, even providing funeral marches. The emotional extremes of late romanticism were never more expansively spelled out. I’d propose that Mahler was consciously or unconsciously also plumbing human emotions in their many extremes, so artfully alluded to in his orchestra and singers. Why else, in Part I alone, San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen the sequence of assertive horns, funeral march, sunny trombone solo, dissonance, upbeat march (a la ”Star Wars”), total exuberance, tempo shifts, and a murky, pensive transition toward marches both depressing and upbeat? For this grandest of season finales however, it finished with sheer bliss June 28, Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen dashing upstage and hugging his soloists on trumpet (Aaron Schuman) and trombone (Timothy Higgins), who both came through splendiferously. The trumpeter had a dual role, also playing a cornet offstage to simulate the post horn. Part Two is a four-movement smorgasbord. It ranged from the mezzo Kelley O’Connor’s interpretation of an ultra-soft Nietzsche midnight poem to an exuberant 50-member women’s and youth chorus, combined, for the crowning Angels’ Song. By then, if the Gates of Heaven don’t actually open up, at the very least Mahler had completed his biggest composition ever, presumably heralding enough income to pay for those bucolic and inspiring lakeside summers near Salzburg. MUSIC NOTES The financial plight of the debt-ravaged SF Symphony, had the musicians once again leafletting patrons as they arrived. While voicing their strong support of Salonen, hoping that he will delay his announced 2025 departure, they also deplore the program cutbacks at SFS, done to reduce the growing deficits. The SFS debts, prompting Salonen’s 2025 departure, has gotten media attention as far away as New York City….The oddity of conductor Salonen’s sitting down for a five-minute break between parts one and two were not due to fatigue, but rather a specification in the score – perhaps more motivated for the perspiring musicians than the conductor. S.F. SYMPHONY and choruses under Salonen in Symphony No. 3 of Mahler June 28-30, Davies Hall, San Francisco. SFS season finale. For SFS info: (415) 864-6000, or go online, www. sfsymphony.org .

articles.text: David Finckel and Wu Han at Music@Menlo Tickets are available now for the annual Music@Menlo concerts, with performances beginning July 19. From July 19 to August 10, Music@Menlo’s 22nd season celebrates French chamber music and its impact across the globe, featuring 44 artists including 13 festival debuts and music spanning 300 years. The internationally acclaimed chamber music festival was founded by David Finckel and Wu Han. Inaugurated in 2003 at Menlo School, the festival features concerts, lectures, and a training program for aspiring professional musicians. The festival’s mission is to engage and sustain an audience for chamber music that is programmed, presented, and performed at the highest level of artistic excellence. Concert programs are performed by a collection of the greatest chamber musicians around the world, provided in intimate settings at Menlo School and Spieker Center for the Arts. articles.text: Marion Cotillard and Owen Wilson in Midnight in Paris Woody Allen is a serial monogamist when it comes to world-class cities. He fell in love with New York, then London, briefly Spain, and now Paris. Ah, Paris. Allen caresses its wide boulevards and avenues, reveals skylines under a startling blue sky, captures the wide sidewalks, damp from rain, the busy outdoor cafes, the lovely restaurants and grand lobbies of hotels. From the first frame of Midnight in Paris, photographed by the gifted cinematographer Darius Khondji, Allen gives the city of lights a lingering embrace that ripples throughout the film. Gil Pender (Owen Wilson) and his fiancée, Inez (Rachel McAdams), have joined her parents (Kurt Fuller and Mimi Kennedy) in Paris. Gil is enchanted by the city, wants to walk the streets in the rain – especially the rain – and waxes nostalgic about what he believes were the glorious 1920s, the golden age when writers and artists, known as the Lost Generation, took up residence. A screenwriter in Hollywood, Gil tells Inez that he would love to move to Paris, find inspiration, and work on his novel – his protagonist owns a nostalgia shop filled with memorabilia. Inez, a lovely, mercenary young woman with the heart of a philistine, doesn’t grasp anything that Gil is attempting to convey, nor do her suspicious, judgmental parents. So instead of spending time going to clubs with Inez, he wanders the streets of Paris into the midnight hours. And it’s on one such late night peregrination, feeling lost, literally and figuratively, that a classic Peugeot town car stops and a couple, formally dressed, insist that he join them. And so begins Gil’s journey back to that period about which he has romanticized, meeting a host of writers and artists to include Gertrude Stein (Kathy Bates), Ernest Hemingway (Corey Stoll) and the Fitzgeralds, F. Scott (Tom Hiddleston) and Zelda (Alison Pill). These moments are wonderfully rendered, Gil’s jaw constantly dropping in astonishment, his heart given a tumble when he meets the lovely Adriana (Marion Cottillard), current girlfriend of Pablo Picasso (Marcial Di Fonzo Bo). It’s all pretty heady stuff with background music by Cole Porter. But there is a nugget of Woody Allen wisdom tucked into this engaging narrative, and it has to do with the nudging belief that plagues us all – well, perhaps many of us – that the past is always qualitatively better than the present. For Gil it’s Paris of the 20s. For others, it might be pre-industrial America, or the early 40s when America was on the cusp of World War II. Some have referred to those who stepped forward during this period as the “greatest generation.” A nice bit of nostalgia. This slim but important insight offered up by Midnight in Paris – which is seamlessly presented with laugh-out-loud moments – is that we have but one life to live and if it’s going to be lived fully it’s best to live it in the present. A nice thought that resonates, offered up by Gil, who is an uncanny doppelganger for Woody in mannerisms and pacing, conveying just a hint of Allen’s signature nebbish uncertainty. This film is one of Allen’s best since Match Point. It’s richly put together, with a strong sense that the auteur is back on his game. Which is all to the good. Midnight in Paris. Written and directed by Woody Allen. Starring Owen Wilson, Rachel McAdams, Marion Cotillard. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Fandango/Prime.

articles.text: Let’s get a round-trip ticket from Heaven to Hell. Sounds like a great adventure, doesn’t it? That is what happened at a concert on Sunday in San Francisco. I neglected to realize that Sunday was Pride Day in San Francisco. “The City” loves its rainbow-hued celebration. It was a red- flag day for sigalerts. The streets were clogged with idling cars. As the traffic stalled, we heard Bronx cheers from snails as they sped past the halted cars. Traffic was at a standstill. You could see the smoke coming from the ears of the drivers. There was a very interesting concert at St. Mary’s Cathedral which was scheduled to begin at 4 p.m. We finally arrived, albeit late, for the concert’s opening. Frustration was the most appropriate word. The concert was in progress. My first thought was: “this sounds like hell!“ I looked at the program and sure enough the first piece was “Hell” from Three Symphonic Chorales by Sigfrid Karg-Elert (1877-1933). Seated at the grand console of the organ was St. Mary’s outstanding organist, Christoph Tietze. There was a small audience in St. Mary’s spacious Cathedral. The absentees missed an outstanding concert. As Tieze continued his program, I began to realize that we were listening to imaginative tonal colors and dramatic dynamics. Just as a fine orchestra needs a great conductor to inspire it, so does a grand organ need an imaginative organist. That’s what we got on Sunday. The German composer Sigfrid Karg-Elert is not a famous name. I cannot say that he is one of my favorite composers, but he certainly is imaginative. The entire concert was dedicated to works by this German composer with his Swedish-spelled name. As for the music, it ranged from heavenly to hellish, soloistic to cacophonic – and everything in between…often taking the listener into the beyond. Marion Cotillard and Owen Wilson in Midnight in Paris By Chris Honoré Woody Allen is a serial monogamist when it comes to world-class cities. He fell in love with New York, then London, briefly Spain, and now Paris. Ah, Paris. Allen caresses its wide boulevards and avenues, reveals skylines under a startling blue sky, captures the wide sidewalks, damp from rain, the busy outdoor cafes, the lovely restaurants and grand lobbies of hotels. From the first frame of Midnight in Paris, photographed by the gifted cinematographer Darius Khondji, Allen gives the city of lights a lingering embrace that ripples throughout the film. Gil Pender (Owen Wilson) and his fiancée, Inez (Rachel McAdams), have joined her parents (Kurt Fuller and Mimi Kennedy) in Paris. Gil is enchanted by the city, wants to walk the streets in the rain – especially the rain – and waxes nostalgic about what he believes were the glorious 1920s, the golden age when writers and artists, known as the Lost Generation, took up residence. A screenwriter in Hollywood, Gil tells Inez that he would love to move to Paris, find inspiration, and work on his novel – his protagonist owns a nostalgia shop filled with memorabilia. Inez, a lovely, mercenary young woman with the heart of a philistine, doesn’t grasp anything that Gil is attempting to convey, nor do her suspicious, judgmental parents. So instead of spending time going to clubs with Inez, he wanders the streets of Paris into the midnight hours. And it’s on one such late night peregrination, feeling lost, literally and figuratively, that a classic Peugeot town car stops and a couple, formally dressed, insist that he join them. And so begins Gil’s journey back to that period about which he has romanticized, meeting a host of writers and artists to include Gertrude Stein (Kathy Bates), Ernest Hemingway (Corey Stoll) and the Fitzgeralds, F. Scott (Tom Hiddleston) and Zelda (Alison Pill). These moments are wonderfully rendered, Gil’s jaw constantly dropping in astonishment, his heart given a tumble when he meets the lovely Adriana (Marion Cottillard), current girlfriend of Pablo Picasso (Marcial Di Fonzo Bo). It’s all pretty heady stuff with background music by Cole Porter. But there is a nugget of Woody Allen wisdom tucked into this engaging narrative, and it has to do with the nudging belief that plagues us all – well, perhaps many of us – that the past is always qualitatively better than the present. For Gil it’s Paris of the 20s. For others, it might be pre-industrial America, or the early 40s when America was on the cusp of World War II. Some have referred to those who stepped forward during this period as the “greatest generation.” A nice bit of nostalgia. This slim but important insight offered up by Midnight in Paris – which is seamlessly presented with laugh-out-loud moments – is that we have but one life to live and if it’s going to be lived fully it’s best to live it in the present. A nice thought that resonates, offered up by Gil, who is an uncanny doppelganger for Woody in mannerisms and pacing, conveying just a hint of Allen’s signature nebbish uncertainty. This film is one of Allen’s best since Match Point. It’s richly put together, with a strong sense that the auteur is back on his game. Which is all to the good. Midnight in Paris. articles.text: Kyle Chandler, Joel Courtney, Elle Fanning and Ron Eldard in Super 8 Super 8 is a great movie. What makes it great is the story, a solid coming of age tale of four boys and a girl, all on the cusp of adolescence, all set free from school, eager to begin their summer project: the shooting of a super 8 monster movie. And so, on a balmy night at midnight, having snuck out of their respective houses, they drive (don’t ask) to the local railroad station and under a canopy of stars, the camera on a tripod, begin shooting their film. That is until they hear a train in the distance. Charley (Riley Griffith), the director, tells his crew to wait. He wants the train for background. And so the kids wait, the light of the train growing larger, the noise of the locomotive reaching them. And it’s at that moment something happens that sends the narrative in a profoundly different direction. It’s a huge shift, delivered with a riveting crash. The movie quote that comes to mind is from Jaws, when Roy Scheider, small town sheriff, standing on the stern of a trawler, sees the enormous shark for the first time. Eyes wide, he backs toward the wheel house and says, “I think we’re going to need a bigger boat.” Super 8 is set in 1979 in a small Ohio town. At the center of the kids’ adventure is Joe Lamb (Joel Courtney), 12-years-old. He has recently lost his mother in an accident at the steel mill. His father, town deputy Jack Lamb (Kyle Chandler), is remote and, like Joe, still grieving. Joe finds solace with his friends; the prospect of spending the summer making a monster movie offers a way to escape the wrenching loss he has experienced. It also helps that Charley has asked Alice Dainard (Elle Fanning) to act in the film, Alice being a girl that Joe has admired from afar but never dared speak to. For Super 8 to work, Abrams has to get the story and the kids just right. And he does, which is no small thing. The tale is compelling and the kids are wonderful, each delivering an excellent performance, led by Fanning and newcomer Courtney. The young filmmakers soon learn that they are caught up in circumstances they never could have foreseen and realize that they must rely on one another to survive. Their fear and sense of urgency has an overwhelming sense of verisimilitude, conveyed nicely to the audience. Their dilemma is our dilemma. If this all sounds a bit vague, well, Super 8 is a movie that must be seen fresh, with as little information as possible. Of course, reviews and comments, even the trailer, will conspire to be too informative. But resist. As an aside, the second half of the film proves to be the most difficult. It’s in act three that Abrams must decide how to reveal what is behind the phenomenon that is impacting everyone in town. He handles this moment as well as can be expected. And likely it really doesn’t matter for Abrams has made a terrific summer movie. Super 8. Directed by J.J. Abrams. Starring Kyle Chandler, Elle Fanning, Joel Courtney. 1 hr, 52 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2011. Now streaming on Fandango/Prime/Paramount+.

articles.text: When I saw the trailer for The Aeronauts I was immediately taken. What denotes adventure more than a massively tall, colorful balloon (or better, a sky full of balloons) floating into the distance on unseen currents of wind? And there was the cast, almost exclusively of Felicity Jones as Amelia Wren, balloon pilot, and Eddie Redmayne portraying James Glaisher, a wannabe meteorologist. The year is 1862, so, naturally, pretty much what is known about the weather is gleaned by stepping outside. Jones and Redmayne were wonderful in The Theory of Everything, that wonderful story about Stephen Hawking. They are about to join forces in a great adventure, meaning an attempt to go higher than anyone has before (above 23,000 feet). Their vehicle, so to speak, is a spectacular red and white gas balloon, some 80 feet tall and 55 feet wide (actually made for the production), with a good-sized rectangular wicker basket hanging below, its interior filled with ropes and bags of sand and James’ weather measuring instruments. At the outset of their journey, they bicker; as a team they’re oil and water. James is a bit of a rigid fussbudget. Amelia is an unwilling pilot, disinterested in the techie stuff that is scattered about. After a brief prologue, up they go – but directly into a storm that buffets them about, reminding them and the audience that they are incredibly vulnerable, a mere speck in a sky that is endlessly unpredictable. As they reach the higher elevations, well above 23,000 feet, the air becomes frigidly cold and the air perilously thin. Something they could not have fully anticipated since no one had ever been this high above the earth. But know that for drama, it is the weather and not much more that creates tension. We watch them cope with the unknown as they near the farthest reaches of the atmosphere, while all they have is each other and the confines of the basket, meaning there are long stretches in the tale that feel benign. Benign that is until the moment they realize that they must descend or die. It’s then that they discover that the opening to the balloon, designed to spill the gas, has been frozen shut. And thus begins a nicely riveting ending to act three. But it’s a bit of a wait. The Aeronauts. Directed by Tom Harper. Starring Felicity Jones, Eddie Redmayne, Tom Courtney. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2019. Now streaming on Fandango, Prime / Apple TV. Felicity Jones and Eddie Redmayne in The Aeronauts

articles.text: Chocolate Chip Cookie Cake When my latest edition of Bake from Scratch magazine arrived, this was the first recipe I wanted to bake as it is exactly the kind of sweet treat we enjoy. It is such a hit that I’ve baked it several times, making a few adaptations along the way. This will make frequent appearances over the summer as it both keeps and travels well for picnics, barbeques, block parties, you name it. The texture is firmer than a typical cake but less dense than a brownie. Its crispy edges and softer center mean plenty of texture for all tastes. Chocolate Chip Cookie Cake Adapted from Bake from Scratch, May/June 2024 INGREDIENTS • ½ cup unsalted butter • 1 tablespoon heavy whipping cream • 1⁄3 cup granulated sugar • ¾ cup light brown sugar, lightly packed • 1 large egg, room temperature • 1 large egg yolk, room temperature • 2 teaspoons vanilla extract • 2 cups plus 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour • ½ teaspoon sea salt • ½ teaspoon espresso powder • ½ teaspoon baking powder • ¼ teaspoon baking soda • 1 cup chocolate chips, preferably dark, but a mix of dark and semi-sweet works too • Garnish: ¼ cup chocolate chips, melted INSTRUCTIONS Prepare a 9-inch springform pan by cutting a round of parchment paper to fit the bottom. Butter the sides. Set aside. Melt butter over medium heat in a small, heavy-bottomed saucepan. Cook until the butter foams and the milk solids turn golden brown. Stir occasionally and do not leave unattended. This takes about 5 minutes. Transfer to a 3-quart, heatproof mixing bowl to cool slightly. Add the heavy cream and cool completely. Photos by Deborah Quok Meanwhile whisk together the flour, salt, espresso powder, baking powder, and baking soda in a small bowl and set aside. When the butter mixture is cooled, add the granulated sugar and beat with a handheld mixer, or in a stand mixer, on medium-high speed. When the granulated sugar is incorporated, add the brown sugar and continue beating on medium-high speed until the mixture is light, fluffy. Stop to scrape the sides of the bowl as needed. Add egg and egg yolk one at a time, beating until combined after each addition. Beat in vanilla extract. The mixture should have at least doubled in volume from the beginning. Add the flour mixture, beating on low speed until just combined. Finish stirring by hand using a spatula as needed to incorporate the flour fully, but don’t overmix. Fold in the chocolate chips to disperse evenly. Transfer the dough into the prepared baking pan and gently pat into an even layer. Cover with cling wrap and refrigerate overnight or up to 3 days. Position an oven rack to the middle oven position. Preheat to 350° F. Bake until the edges of the cake are golden brown and top looks dry, about 40 – 45 minutes. Remove from the oven and let cool for 10 minutes, at which time remove the sides from the springform pan. Cool completely before garnishing and serving. Garnish: Optional as the cookie cake looks appealing as is. But to fancy it up, melt ¼ cup of chocolate chips in a small, heatproof ramekin (a few short bursts in the microwave works here). Use a small spoon, knife tip or wooden skewer to dip into the melted chocolate and spread onto the cookie cake as desired. Store in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers take a group photo at the intersection of Mountain and Bellevue Avenue, where a live oak has been planted to replace an historic Sequoia tree that was dying. Participating in last week’s walk were: Avelina Buijs, Karen Glasser, Alicia Rivera, Dave DeRoche, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Denny McGee, Kat Lang, Elizabeth Richter, Carolyn George, Jackie Leventhal, Tina Shum, Stella Houston, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, Greg Slatoff, Joyce Ahern, Jack Fischrup, Sharona Fischrup, Judy Sokoloff, Kat Kewley, Rick Eigenbrode, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Gloria DaSilva, Bob Wong, Bill Ahern, Peggy Shultz, Sean Brient, Janet Laurent, Priscilla Wanerus, Jim Kellogg, Mark Laurent, Claudine Bach, Marianne Jakus, Albert Chen, Chuck Oraftik, Mark Davis, Nancy Henn, Lisa Euphrat, Mary Carter, Charlene Louie, Elane Rehr, Sherry Jacobs, Greg Meyer with K-9 best friend Rumi, Robert Lang, Noemi Alvarado, Lois Price, Brenda Ferrero and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Kathleen Parkerton, a first-time walker. The Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed a strong turnout of 50 walkers and three K-9 best friends last week. Lois Price and Sherry Jacobs reminded the group that they are an official entry in this year’s 4th of July Parade. The City has completed a public tree inventory to catalog the many different species of trees in Piedmont. Dozens of trees were identified that are either failing or have died because of the increasingly harsher climate. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation has begun a campaign to support replacing these trees with species that are native, or compatible to California, and more likely to thrive. The Reforestation Project started in Dracena Park with the removal of more than 30 dead trees. The City’s arborist thinks they died because of the prolonged drought, warmer summers with less fog, and changing climate conditions. The project also included replacing the tall Sequoia in the Mountain-Bellevue circle. The walkers hadn’t been to the circle for a while, so it was the destination this week. The group headed off going through Piedmont Park and stopped by the Japanese Tea House to look at a redwood tree that is clearly not in good health. The walkers went up Sierra Avenue to a hidden path to the Mountain-Bellevue circle where more information was shared. Cameron Wolfe had written that the Sequoia stood high in this intersection for generations, even serving as Piedmont’s first holiday tree during the 20s and 30s but stopped at the onset of World War II. Last fall, there was an immediate danger of the tree toppling and it was thus removed. The Park Commission and the Beautification Foundation approved replacing the Sequoia with an Island Oak. This species is native to California, especially the Channel Islands. The tree is likely to thrive in this small traffic island that has no regular source of water. PBF raised $8,000 from neighbors and the new tree was planted in the circle on June 10. These funds will also cover additional planting, and care for the tree for at least two years. Some walkers went down Sea View, but the rest of the group continued up the steep Mountain Avenue. They enjoyed the beautiful homes along the way, and crossed Blair Avenue to see the wonderful view of San Francisco from Bell Avenue. Peggy Shultz, who lives on Bell, said the street was once the continuation of Mountain Avenue, but someone named Bell wanted the road’s name changed. The group continued down Scenic Avenue to a public stairway 281 feet long and emerged on Blair Avenue, where they saw the house where Jack London wrote The Call of the Wild in 1903. Going up Hardwick Avenue took the walkers to Oakland Avenue and then back to Highland Avenue and the Exedra. It was a two mile walk with trees, elevation, hidden paths, history, views, fun, and friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: The state motto of New Hampshire is also my philosophy for raising chickens. Backyard chicken husbandry has been gaining in popularity for years, driven in part by a backlash against industrial agriculture. Now kept by 10 percent of American households, chickens have become the country’s third most popular pets after dogs and cats. But most of these pet chickens live in backyard cages, even though their owners would probably choose to buy “free range” eggs at the grocery store. Cages aren’t fun for the chickens or their owners, who must clean them out constantly. So when my wife and I bought our first chickens a decade ago, she suggested having them bed down in a small coop at night and during the day roam free all over the backyard. It seemed like a reasonable idea – until the chickens shredded up the flower beds and pooped all over the patio. It turns out that people keep chickens in cages for a reason. A great deal of discussion ensued, with aesthetics at the fore. We finally agreed to relegate the chickens to the rear portion of the forested backyard, where the mix of Algerian ivy, mock orange, and oak trees was chicken proof. We didn’t want to install an unsightly fence, however, so we chose a green wire fence that was less than 3 feet tall and blended in with the foliage. This worked fantastically – for a couple of days. Chickens are ground birds but they actually do fly. Once they figured out how to jump the fence, we were back to where we’d started. Next, I clipped the feathers on the chickens’ wings, to the great consternation of my wife, who did not understand that it’s a painless procedure akin to trimming one’s fingernails. This prevented some of the chickens from hopping the fence. And that’s when I learned certain Our free-range kiddo several years ago with one of our first free-range chickens. You’ll need to cage baby chickens until they’re nearly full-sized. We lost many to hawks. chicken breeds are known to be “flighty,” meaning that even with clipped wings they can get up high in the air. My wife loved the Ameraucanas, a flighty breed that comes from Chile and lays beautiful eggs ranging from green to turquoise. But she didn’t want to herd them back across the fence every day. “Fine,” I told her. “I guess that means I’ll have to eat them.” She promptly enlisted our kids in a campaign to “save the chickens.” I felt a little bad researching how to kill and pluck animals that the kids thought of as pets. Fortunately, the problem worked itself out. The Ameraucanas got eaten by raccoons. I quietly celebrated our loss, but not for long. The raccoons’ welltimed coup de grace marked the beginning of an onslaught against all of the chickens. Though chickens will reliably roost in their coop every night, we’d forget to close the coop door and the next morning find our flock reduced from, My son pictured with our small coop, now controlled by an automatic door. The chickens forage in this area during the day.

articles.text: One of the keen pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it afterward. That’s just what Piedmont’s Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting and then a discussion of it afterward. This month’s film is the sizzling 1959 American comedy, Some Like It Hot, directed by Billy Wilder and starring Marilyn Monroe, Jack Lemmon and Tony Curtis. Adding to the fun are two stars who came out of retirement to lend their talents: George Raft as the bad guy and the great Joe E. Brown. The tale starts off with a bang: machine gun fire in 1920s Chicago. After accidentally witnessing a Mafia massacre, saxophone player Joe (Tony Curtis) and his long-suffering buddy, Jerry (Jack Lemmon), improvise a quick plan to escape town with their lives. Disguising themselves as women, they join an all-female band and hop a train bound for sunny Florida. While Joe pretends to be a millionaire to win the band’s sexy singer, Sugar (Marilyn Monroe), Jerry finds himself pursued by a real millionaire (Joe E. Brown) as things heat up and the mobsters, headed by the snake-eyed Spats (George Raft) close in. Nominated for seven Academy Awards, Some Like It Hot received widespread acclaim from critics and audiences alike, and is considered among the best films of all time. Roger Ebert said of it, “Wilder’s comedy is one of the enduring treasures of the movies, a film of inspiration and meticulous craft.” In 1989, the movie became one of the first 25 inducted into the U.S. National Film Registry. In 1999, Entertainment Weekly voted it number nine on their list of “100 Greatest Movies.” It was voted the top comedy movie ever by the American Film Institute. Some Like It Hot offers many pleasures, among them the best and funniest closing line of any movie: “Nobody’s perfect,” uttered with a smile of heavenly silliness by Joe E. Brown on a racing speedboat. This is not a spoiler. You have to see the movie to understand how funny the line is. Some Like It Hot will be screened on Thursday, July 11th, at a one-time Flix Fest starting time of 3:30. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the event takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors for this showing will open at 3:00. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration may be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is Chinese director Zhang Zimou’s much honored 1994 drama, To Live. It will be shown on August 8th, at the usual time of 1:00 p.m. Movie poster from Some Like It Hot

articles.text: Preserving the Summer Harvest Preserved summer flowers crafted into framed art Now that it’s officially summer, the best part of gardening is here - harvesting. From tomatoes to corn, summer brings the freshest crops from a home garden and the farmers market. Here are a few fun ways I like to preserve the taste of the season. We’re lucky enough to have both a plum and apricot tree in our yard that produce generously each season. While fresh fruit from the tree is incredible, my favorite way to preserve stone fruit and berries from our garden is by canning a fresh fruit jam. articles.text: A novel by Chris Honoré INTRODUCTION The intended audience for the novel The Journey of Max Braverman, written by Chris Honoré, is preteens and early adolescents. The Piedmont Post is providing weekly installments of the book to encourage reading by young people. Hopefully, young readers will embrace the story, which focuses on the close relationship between two young brothers, Max and Jordie. The setting is a central California town in the mid-sixties. The novel is available through Barnes & Noble and Amazon. PART 1 - Jordie Jordie believed he could fly. I’d just come home from Marty’s and walked down the driveway into the backyard and saw him standing on the roof of the garage, his arms forward, feet together like he was balancing on the edge of a diving board. “Jordie,” I yelled. “Don’t you move. Don’t you do anything. I’m not kidding.” “Watch this, Max,” he called down, his reedy voice excited, his eyes looking straight ahead, already seeing himself in full flight, buzzing treetops. “Watch nothing, Jordie. You listen to me. I’m not kidding around. There is no way.” Jordie stood very still, his face scrunched in concentration, his skinny legs bent at the knees, every muscle tight, committed, ready to go airborne. The problem started when our mom made him this terrific orange cape with a silver lightning bolt down the back. It looked exactly like the one that Captain Marvel wore, a comic book superhero that Jordie couldn’t stop talking about. She’d given it to him as a surprise and when he opened the box and took out that amazing cape, all silver and orange, flaring wide at the bottom, well, she and I realized right then that maybe it hadn’t been such a good idea. See, Jordie got this look in his eyes, like all he had to do was put that cape on and he could levitate. Leap tall buildings. Run around the block faster than a speeding bullet. Or launch himself off the garage roof. And when our mom draped it over his shoulders and buttoned the strap, I had this feeling that Jordie was already planning his first flight. “Jordie, here’s the deal,” I yelled up at him. “If you don’t get down off that roof right now, I’m coming up there and throw you off and you’ll see that people can’t fly, no matter what they’re wearing. I mean, think about it. That’s why they take the damn bus to work. And if you jump, I’ll have to use that cape to wrap up your broken arm. I’m not fooling around. Swear. You will break something if you do this. Like a brick, Jord. Straight down.” Jordie stood there, weighing what I’d said, wanting with all his heart to give that cape a try, but the look on his face told me that he was starting to think about the role gravity played in our lives. Seeing an opening, I yelled, “I swear to God, Jord, this is no bull, you couldn’t fly a foot if you were wearing ten capes. Now will you please knock this off and get down.” Finally, muttering and complaining, he walked slowly to the back of the garage where he’d set up a ladder and crawled down, all the while telling me he could’ve done it. If I’d just keep my big nose out of stuff, it would’ve worked. I told Jordie to put a lid on it and how about starting with flying from our bedroom to the bathroom and back. If that worked, he could get back up on the garage and I’d even hold the ladder. Jordie was like no one else, I swear. Take his height. Weeks would go by and not a peep about it. Then, suddenly, it was a very big deal. More than once he’d refused to come in for dinner, and I’d find him sitting up in the huge oak tree in our backyard, his baseball cap on backwards, never a good sign, his thin body wedged between the branches, sulking. And Jordie could sulk like no one else. Though I have to say he didn’t hold a candle next to Howard, this guy who lived with us for a while. He was the sulking champ of the world, no contest. and sure enough, there he’d be. “Jord, mom wants you to come in for dinner.” “I’ve stopped growing, Max.” “What?” “I’m not getting any taller.” “Yes you are, Jord.” “I’m not. I swear. I can tell. Not an inch.” “Jordie, come on, just get down. You haven’t stopped growing. You’re growing every day. Really.” “How can you tell?” “Look, here’s how it works. The person growing? They can’t tell they’re growing. Other people, who’re watching, they can tell. Think about it. What does Aunt Celia say every time she sees you? She says, ‘Well, look at you, Jordan, look how much you’ve grown.’ Remember how she always says that? You think you’re not and she can tell you are. Celia’s watching. From the outside. You, the one growing, you’re watching from the inside. Inside doesn’t count. Now, will you get down outta that tree and come in and eat? Mom’s waiting for us.” “Fine. But after dinner, you have to measure me. And no mooshing down the hair this time. articles.text: Piedmont police noticed a vehicle driving in the middle of the night on Vista Avenue with a covered-up license plate on Monday, June 17. The vehicle, a 2001 blue Jaguar S-type, was being driven by a suspect known to the Piedmont Police. When officers pursued the vehicle, the suspect jumped out of the vehicle and fled on foot onto Bonita Avenue. Police were unable to locate the suspect, who had a $10,000 misdemeanor arrest warrant for narcotics out of Alameda County Sheriff’s Office. The vehicle was abandoned by the driver on Vista Ave, not far from the police station. Inside the vehicle was “a large volume of property.” Thirty-eight items in total were inside the vehicle; the items came from several stolen packages. Fifteen items were returned. The suspect’s vehicle was towed away and any other found property that could not be returned was booked as evidence at the Police Department. The suspect is still at large and charges are pending.
